preamble.summary: A reflection on death -- bitter to the prosperous, welcome to the suffering -- followed by the fate of the wicked whose memory perishes. The chapter then develops a nuanced catalog of shame: certain things are rightly shameful (sin, dishonesty, injustice), while other things are wrongly considered shameful (as explored in chapter 42).
preamble.remarkable: The opening meditation on death (vv. 1-7) is among the most philosophically mature passages in Sirach, acknowledging that death's meaning depends entirely on the life it ends. The shame catalog (vv. 14-27) functions as a kind of moral inventory, inviting self-examination across the full range of social and private conduct.
preamble.friction: The text's view of death as final ('in Sheol there is no reproof of life,' v. 7 in some numberings) sits uneasily alongside later Jewish and Christian resurrection theology. Ben Sira's anthropology here is firmly pre-resurrection.
preamble.connections: Ecclesiastes 7:1 (the day of death better than the day of birth); Job 3 (Job's wish that he had never been born); Proverbs 10:7 (the memory of the righteous is a blessing); Psalm 49 (the futility of wealth before death).

verses.text_latin: O mors quam amara est memoria tua homini pacem habenti in substantiis suis.
verses.rendering: O death, how bitter is the thought of you to a man at peace amid his possessions.
translator_notes: One of the most quoted verses in Sirach. The apostrophe to death personifies it as an intruder upon comfort and security.

key_terms.note: Not merely recollection but the present awareness of death's approach; the mind's anticipation of its own ending.

verses.text_latin: Viro quieto et cuius viae directae sunt in omnibus et adhuc valenti accipere cibum.
verses.rendering: To a man who is at rest, whose ways are prosperous in all things, and who still has the strength to enjoy food.
translator_notes: Three markers of the good life: tranquility, prosperity, and appetite. Death threatens all three simultaneously.

verses.text_latin: O mors bonum est iudicium tuum homini indigenti et qui minoratur viribus.
verses.rendering: O death, your sentence is welcome to a man in want and whose strength is failing.
translator_notes: The counterpoint: for the destitute and exhausted, death is a release, not a terror.

key_terms.note: Death's decree; here experienced as merciful judgment rather than punishment.

verses.text_latin: Defecto aetate et cui de omnibus cura est et incredibili qui perdit patientiam.
verses.rendering: To the aged and failing, consumed with worry over all things, to the despairing one who has lost all patience.
translator_notes: Four conditions that make death welcome: advanced age, declining health, constant anxiety, and exhausted hope.

verses.text_latin: Noli metuere iudicium mortis memento quae ante te fuerunt et quae superventura sunt tibi hoc iudicium a Domino omni carni.
verses.rendering: Do not fear the sentence of death; remember those who went before you and those who will come after. This is the Lord's decree for all flesh.
translator_notes: A Stoic-resonant consolation: death is universal, shared by all who preceded and all who will follow. Its universality should neutralize its terror.

key_terms.note: Death is not random fate but divinely appointed; accepting it as God's decree transforms resignation into submission.

verses.text_latin: Et quid superveniet tibi in beneplacito Altissimi sive decem sive centum sive mille anni.
verses.rendering: And what will come upon you is according to the pleasure of the Most High, whether ten or a hundred or a thousand years.
translator_notes: The span of life, whether short or long, is determined by God's will. The range from ten to a thousand years encompasses the full biblical spectrum of longevity.

verses.text_latin: Non est enim in inferno accusatio vitae.
verses.rendering: For in the grave there is no reproof of life.
translator_notes: Once dead, no one can be called to account -- or call others to account. The grave silences all disputation.

key_terms.note: Infernus renders Sheol, the shadowy underworld of the dead in Hebrew thought -- not the later Christian concept of hell as a place of punishment.

verses.text_latin: Filii abominationum fiunt filii peccatorum et qui conversantur secus domos impiorum.
verses.rendering: The children of sinners become children of abomination, as do those who dwell near the houses of the ungodly.
translator_notes: Association with the wicked corrupts: proximity to sin deforms the next generation.

key_terms.note: Those whose character has been deformed by the influence of wicked parents or neighbors; the moral contagion of sin.

verses.text_latin: Filiorum peccatorum periet hereditas et cum semine illorum adsiduitas obprobrii.
verses.rendering: The inheritance of sinners' children will perish, and with their offspring enduring reproach.

verses.text_latin: De patre impio queruntur filii quoniam propter illum sunt in obprobrio.
verses.rendering: Children complain about an ungodly father, because on his account they bear reproach.
translator_notes: A poignant social observation: children suffer the reputational consequences of their parents' wickedness.

verses.text_latin: Vae vobis viri impii qui dereliquistis legem Dei Altissimi.
verses.rendering: Woe to you, ungodly men, who have abandoned the law of God Most High!
translator_notes: A prophetic 'woe' oracle inserted into wisdom discourse -- Ben Sira blends genres freely.

verses.text_latin: Et si nati fueritis in maledictionibus nascemini et si mortui fueritis in maledictionibus erit pars vestra.
verses.rendering: When you are born, you are born under a curse, and when you die, a curse will be your portion.
translator_notes: The wicked are cursed from birth to death -- their entire existence is bracketed by malediction.

key_terms.note: The covenant curse (Deuteronomy 28:15-68) that falls upon those who abandon the Torah.

verses.text_latin: Omnia quae de terra sunt in terram convertentur sic impii a maledicto in perditionem.
verses.rendering: Everything that comes from the earth returns to the earth; so the ungodly go from curse to destruction.
translator_notes: A reprise of 40:11, but with a grimmer application: the wicked's return to dust is not merely natural but penal.

verses.text_latin: Luctus hominum in corpore ipsorum nomen autem impiorum delebitur.
verses.rendering: The grief of mankind is over their bodies, but the name of the ungodly will be blotted out.
translator_notes: Physical death mourns the body; moral death erases the name. The loss of one's name is worse than the loss of one's life.

verses.text_latin: Curam habe de bono nomine hoc enim magis permanebit tibi quam mille thesauri pretiosi et magni.
verses.rendering: Take care of your good name, for it will endure for you longer than a thousand great and precious treasures.
translator_notes: Reputation as the most durable form of wealth -- a cornerstone of Ben Sira's ethical teaching.

key_terms.note: Shem tov in Hebrew: a reputation for integrity that survives the person who built it.

verses.text_latin: Bonae vitae numerus dierum boni autem nominis permanebunt in aevum.
verses.rendering: A good life has its number of days, but a good name endures forever.

verses.text_latin: Disciplinam in pace conservate filii sapientia enim abscondita et thesaurus invisus quae utilitas in utrisque.
verses.rendering: Preserve discipline in peace, my children; for hidden wisdom and an unseen treasure -- what use is there in either?
translator_notes: Wisdom must be shared, not hoarded. Hidden wisdom is as useless as buried treasure -- both fail to serve their purpose.

key_terms.note: Training and instruction in wisdom; something to be preserved and transmitted, not merely possessed.

verses.text_latin: Melior est homo qui abscondit stultitiam suam quam homo qui abscondit sapientiam suam.
verses.rendering: Better is the one who hides his foolishness than the one who hides his wisdom.
translator_notes: A witty paradox: concealing stupidity is at least socially useful, while concealing wisdom is a moral failure.

verses.text_latin: Ergo reveremini in his quae procedunt de ore meo.
verses.rendering: Therefore have reverence for what proceeds from my mouth.
translator_notes: Ben Sira claims authority for the shame catalog that follows: it deserves serious attention.

verses.text_latin: Non est enim omnem reverentiam observare bonum et non omnia omnibus bene placent in fide.
verses.rendering: For it is not good to observe every kind of shame, and not all things are approved by all in good faith.
translator_notes: The key principle: shame is not uniform. Some things rightly cause shame; others are wrongly stigmatized. Discernment is required.

verses.text_latin: Erubescite a patre et a matre de fornicatione et a praesidente et a potente de mendacio.
verses.rendering: Be ashamed before father and mother of sexual immorality, and before a ruler and a powerful person of lying.
translator_notes: The shame catalog begins: specific sins matched to the social relationships they violate.

key_terms.note: Broad term for illicit sexual conduct; the shame is heightened by its occurrence before one's parents.

verses.text_latin: A principe et a iudice de delicto a synagoga et plebe de iniquitate.
verses.rendering: Before a prince and a judge, be ashamed of an offense; before the assembly and the people, of wrongdoing.

key_terms.note: The gathered community for judicial and religious purposes; in this period, not yet the dedicated building of later Judaism.

verses.text_latin: A socio et amico de iniustitia et de loco in quo habitas.
verses.rendering: Before a companion and friend, be ashamed of injustice, and before the place where you dwell.

verses.text_latin: De furto a veritate Dei et testamento de discubitu in panibus ab obfuscatione dati et accepti.
verses.rendering: Be ashamed of theft before the truth of God and his covenant; of leaning on your elbows over bread; of stinginess in giving and receiving.
translator_notes: A mixture of moral sins (theft, covenant violation) and social gaffes (poor table manners, miserliness). Ben Sira treats both as matters of legitimate shame.

verses.text_latin: A salutantibus de silentio de respectu mulieris fornicariae et ab aversione vultus cognati.
verses.rendering: Be ashamed of silence before those who greet you, of gazing at a woman of loose morals, and of turning away from a kinsman.

verses.text_latin: Ne avertas faciem a proximo tuo et ab auferendo partem et non restituendo.
verses.rendering: Do not turn your face from your neighbor; be ashamed of taking a portion and not returning it.

verses.text_latin: Ne respicias mulierem alieni viri et ne scruteris ancillam eius ne steteris ad lectum eius.
verses.rendering: Do not gaze at another man's wife, and do not meddle with his maidservant; do not stand by her bed.
translator_notes: A progression of increasingly transgressive acts: looking, interfering, and physical proximity -- each step closer to adultery.

verses.text_latin: Ab amicis de sermonibus inproperii et cum dederis ne inproperes.
verses.rendering: Be ashamed before friends of insulting words, and when you have given, do not reproach.
translator_notes: Giving followed by reproach negates the gift. Generosity must be complete -- both in the act and in the attitude that follows.

key_terms.note: To cast the gift back in the recipient's face by reminding them of their debt; a social vice that destroys the relationship the gift was meant to build.
